messages.subject: map() vs. lapply()
parts:
Hi all,

Yesterday, during the tidyverse talk, Michael showed the speed advantage of the map function vs the lapply function: 

df = data_frame(fun = rep(c(lapply, map), 2),
                n = rep(c(1e5, 1e7), each = 2),
                comp_time = map2(fun, n, ~system.time(.x(1:.y, sqrt))))
df$comp_time
## [[1]]
##    user  system elapsed 
##   0.042   0.003   0.046 
## 
## [[2]]
##    user  system elapsed 
##   0.055   0.001   0.059 
## 
## [[3]]
##    user  system elapsed 
##  12.366   0.218  12.612 
## 
## [[4]]
##    user  system elapsed 
##   8.572   0.117   8.742

It seemed strange to me, since both call out to C and should be very fast. I suspected the culprit was wrapping the functions inside a tidyverse function. For comparison, I ran the tests from the presentation, then each test independently.

> df = data_frame(fun = rep(c(lapply, map), 2),
+                 n = rep(c(1e5, 1e7), each = 2),
+                 comp_time = map2(fun, n, ~system.time(.x(1:.y, sqrt))))

>df$comp_time
[[1]]
   user  system elapsed 
  0.034   0.006   0.040 

[[2]]
   user  system elapsed 
  0.040   0.000   0.041 

[[3]]
   user  system elapsed 
 13.297   0.146  13.445 

[[4]]
   user  system elapsed 
  8.963   0.193   9.159 

>system.time(lapply(1:1e5, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.037   0.000   0.035 
>system.time(map(1:1e5, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.040   0.000   0.041 
>system.time(lapply(1:1e7, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed 
  7.400   0.040   7.439 
>system.time(map(1:1e7, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed 
  6.907   0.123   7.032 


Looks like they are about even when not wrapped in a call to map2, with map() a hair faster for larger vectors.

Then for fun, I pre-allocated the large vector:

> x = 1:1e7
> system.time(lapply(x, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed 
  7.320   0.010   7.335 
> system.time(map(x, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed 
   7.69    0.00    7.69 

Lapply comes out a hair ahead with the pre-allocated vector.

Lastly, both vs. a vectorized call:

> system.time(sqrt(x))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.040   0.000   0.038 

Short story: 
 - benchmarking is tough
 - lapply and map are probably equally fast.
 - figuring out vectorized function calls in R is well worth it. 

Hope someone finds this useful.

messages.author: 6e4e37c602c2b104
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: map() vs. lapply()
parts:
Interesting. Benchmarking can indeed be tricky, in part because the measurements are noisy. And as we discussed yesterday, for almost everyone, the time spent coding easily eclipses execution difference. For example, I just spent more time digging into this than I am likely to ever make up from what I learned. :)

I’ll say I definitely agree that finding ways to do vectorizable things with vectorized functions is important. Learning how to do that is a big part of learning to “think in R”. Duncan’s car-moving exercise (here if anyone wants an R challenge!) is a great example of that. I don’t see the tidyverse functions moving learners away from vectorization, but I’d like to hear if others disagree.

To these benchmarks. I just tested five common tasks in base vs tidyverse, each replicated 10 times on data.frames with 1e5, 1e6, or 1e7 rows. Here are the results (means over ten replicates), followed by the code. 

library(tidyverse)

reps = 10
dir.create("temp")

ns = c(n100000 = 1e5, n1000000 = 1e6, n10000000 = 1e7)
rats = 
  lapply(ns, function(n) {
    d = data.frame(x = 1:n, y = rnorm(n))

    tidy = c(
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        data_frame(x = 1:n, y = rnorm(n))
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        filter(d, y > 0)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        mutate(d, z = x * y)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        map(d$x, `^`, -2:2)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        write_csv(d, "temp/temp.csv")
      }))[3, ])
    )

    base = c(
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        data.frame(x = 1:n, y = rnorm(n))
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        d[d$y > 0, ]
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        d$x * d$y
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        lapply(d$x, `^`, -2:2)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        write.csv(d, "temp/temp.csv")
      }))[3, ])
    )

    return(list(tidy = tidy, base = base))
  })

map_df(rats, ~ log(.$tidy / .$base, base = 2)) %>%
  data.frame(fun = c("make-df", "subset-rows", "make-column", "lapply/map", "write-csv")) %>%
  gather(rows, tidy_base, -fun) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fun, y = tidy_base, color = rows)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  coord_flip() + 
  scale_y_continuous(name = "",
                     breaks = -2:2, labels = c("4x\ntidyverse faster", "2x", "even", "2x", "4x\nbase faster")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 18) +
  xlab("")
​

-- 
Michael Levy

messages.author: 9c494544ae7f483f
messages.subject: Re: map() vs. lapply()
parts:
library(microbenchmark)

test <- t(data.frame(runif(1e6), rnorm(1e6)))

microbenchmark(
map(test,sum),
lapply(test,sum),
    ldply(test, sum)
)

Unit: milliseconds
         expr              min              lq              mean         median           uq         max
map(test, sum)    1036.2103   1210.232   1366.307   1308.872   1476.016    2244.916
lapply(test, sum)  968.9341    1234.384    1400.797   1341.150   1542.184    2170.655
ldply(test, sum)    6118.9552  7122.207    7626.764   7510.990   8046.043   10374.573


Arguably no real speed up for this use case (weird that `ldply` was so far off, right? I also tried `laply` with even greater diffs). 

Michael's right though that it largely depends on task. The `tidyverse` seems like it has some nice convenience functions, but it does seem a bit tenuous to hype up the speed as a selling point.

messages.author: 6e4e37c602c2b104
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: map() vs. lapply()
parts:
Right, the plyr functions were kind of notoriously slow. ggplot is too, for now. There was a tradeoff of the convenience of ldply vs. do.call(rbind, lapply) being faster. My argument for the tidyverse is really that you gain convenience without losing execution speed. And as bonus, for some functions you actually do get a speed bump.

But the real case for the tidyverse, in my opinion, is that beginners can get up and running faster and with fewer headaches, and the code is more readable. Whether R instruction should start with tidyverse or base is a question I think about a lot. It came up in several sessions at useR this summer, and I’d enjoy talking more about it if anyone is so inclined.

ps. The tidyverse talk from the other day is online, but not at the link I originally sent out. It is here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9q7gssUP8UA

​

-- 
Michael Levy

Thanks for the link, Michael. I was disappointed not to be able to
view the talk in real time, but, at the same time, given my vast
experience with Murphy, I wasn't entirely surprised.

Regarding teaching R to beginners, I've thought about this myself and
haven't come to a satisfactory conclusion. Having more or less
mastered the gnarly aspects of base R, it somehow feels like
"cheating" to solve problems the Hadley way. (And as an editorial
comment, some things in the tidyverse just seem a little silly to me:
having "ymd" and "myd", etc., functions in lubridate, for example.)

OTOH, I'm beginning to think that that ship has already sailed.
(Resistance is futile ...) I haven't done a systematic study of the
messages on this list, but my visceral impression is that almost all
of the solutions presented here involve the "tidyverse". Sometimes
Duncan will provide an alternative, base-R solution, but such
solutions (from Duncan or others) are rare.

If there *is* more to be said on this topic, I'd like to hear it.

-- Mike

messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: map() vs. lapply()
parts:
My 2c:

I cannot talk extensively about the ease of teaching the tidyverse vs. base beyond the observation that many people who learn the tidyverse are not actually learning R so much as they are stringing together commands through trial and error until they find something that appears to work. Certainly not all, but many lack much understanding about what they are doing. 

I personally find the tidyverse way of writing code much more difficult to read. Some of the non-standard evaluation and non-standard scoping only adds to this. As for convenience, there is nothing in the tidyverse that I cannot do in base R, and often with much less code written. 

However, my biggest concern with the tidyverse is how much it limits R. For example, tidy data might be great for most use cases, but sometimes data are best arranged wide, in lists of lists, or in some other non-tidy format (and sometimes you don't have a choice). Knowing the basics of indexing and subsetting in base R allows you to tackle data in just about any format. From what I have seen, the same cannot be said for the tidyverse.

Will you have a table faster with the jig? Probably. Can you build anything else? Probably not.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: map() vs. lapply()
parts:
I agree that doing things in a reproducible, programmatic way, whether that means using R (tidyverse, base, whatever) or some other tool chain (Python, Julia, etc.) is beneficial. If you are just learning R, this discussion is a bit academic. Likewise, my observation about stringing together commands is just my experience from helping people with their code (but one I have had repeatedly). 

I do think it is helpful for people new to R to be aware of this discussion, however. The tidyverse is often "sold" to people new to R as the latest, greatest, and sometimes only way to use R. The reality is that it is a trade-off. 

When I was learning R, I loved many of what are now core components of the tidyverse. Within a year, I was butting up against their limitations and their use turned from joy to frustration. I ended up having to relearn parts of my workflow to overcome this. If I were concerned with the most efficient use of my time to learn R, this "proto-tidyverse" was wrong for me. You are probably correct that many people will never get to that point and I freely admit that my experience may be atypical, but I think it is good for people to be aware of. It is something I wish I had known 4 years ago.

Matt
